entries.title: Cops release picture of suspect after woman attacked on L platform in Loop
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police are asking for help finding a man who allegedly "battered" a woman on a CTA platform in the Loop earlier this month.</p><p>On Nov. 15, a 54-year-old woman was standing on the Washington/Wabash CTA platform in the Loop around 8:45 a.m. when a man attacked her, police said.</p><p>Anyone with information about the incident is asked to contact Chicago police Public Transportation Detectives at 312-745-4447 or submit an anonymous tip at CPDTIP.com and use reference RD # JK22400.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.title: Latino-focused Tasa Coffee Roasters targeted by social media post alleging ties to ICE
entries.summary: <p>Some community members are calling for a boycott of a popular coffee shop in West Humboldt Park, and workers have walked off the job over a viral social media post alleging the shop has ties to ICE.</p><p>On Monday, the business also was egged.</p><p>Jackie Marquez owns <a class="Link" href="https://www.tasa.coffee/" target="_blank" ><u>Tasa Coffee Roasters</u></a>, a roastery and coffee shop at 4136 W. North Ave. The shop opened in 2022 and quickly became a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/summer-guide/2024/06/22/independently-owned-latino-coffee-shops-serving-up-quality-coffee-bites-and-hospitality-in-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>neighborhood favorite</u></a> for its “Latina-owned and woman-forward” approach.</p><p>But a post that began circulating on social media Monday morning alleges someone with the same name as a man connected to the coffee shop appears in a database of U.S. Department of Homeland Security employees leaked at the end of October.</p><p>WBEZ/Sun-Times can confirm the leaked documents list this individual as having been a supervisory detention and deportation officer at the agency. Public records reviewed by WBEZ/Sun-Times state that an individual by this name has been employed by DHS, but the agency did not provide direct confirmation of his status or position with the agency.</p><p>WBEZ/Sun-Times has been unable to confirm if the man listed in the leak is in fact the same person identified in the viral post, and as a result, is not naming him.</p><p>A search using the Nexis public records database showed an ICE email address and DHS employment location associated with the man’s name. But WBEZ/Sun-Times could not independently confirm the man is, or was ever, employed by ICE.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Egg yolk and shells litter the sidewalk after eggs were thrown at the window of Tasa Coffee Roasters, 4136 W. North Ave. on Monday. The Humboldt Park coffee shop has been the focus of rumors attempting to tie it to Immigration and Customs Enforcement.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The shop’s publicly available business license and grants are all solely in Jackie Marquez’s name. Public records link the couple via mortgage and marriage documents.</p><p>On Monday afternoon, a few neighbors gathered around the shop to get a look at the signs left by workers that read: “After finding out from Reddit that there are allegations … we the baristas and roasters, have closed for the day. We do not stand beside, condone, support or accept anyone or any org associated with ICE. As the baristas, we are discussing what steps will be necessary for us. We intend to do our best as employees to be as honest and transparent as we can be. Thank you.”</p><p>By 4 p.m. Monday, Marquez herself had posted an <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/stories/tasa.coffee.roasters/?hl=en" target="_blank" ><u>Instagram story</u></a> that briefly addressed the situation: “I’m Jackie, the sole owner of Tasa Coffee Roasters. I am a chef. Food and coffee have been my only career. I personally disagree with current immigration policy, and I believe in civil dialogue and mutual respect, even when we disagree. I ask that my employees not be targeted or held responsible for matters outside their control. My commitment remains firmly with my employees, my customers, and my community.”</p><p>Neither Marquez nor the man being targeted had responded to a request for comment by early Monday night.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ab0000" name="image-ab0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5e3ad74/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc3%2F1f%2F7ed48a874ea99940c0b6838b9585%2Fnewtasa-261124-11.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3c32812/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc3%2F1f%2F7ed48a874ea99940c0b6838b9585%2Fnewtasa-261124-11.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7a18a12/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc3%2F1f%2F7ed48a874ea99940c0b6838b9585%2Fnewtasa-261124-11.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Tasa Coffee Roasters, 4136 W. North Ave., in Humboldt Park on Monday, Nov. 23, 2026. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7a18a12/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc3%2F1f%2F7ed48a874ea99940c0b6838b9585%2Fnewtasa-261124-11.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6ccfb30/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc3%2F1f%2F7ed48a874ea99940c0b6838b9585%2Fnewtasa-261124-11.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7a18a12/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc3%2F1f%2F7ed48a874ea99940c0b6838b9585%2Fnewtasa-261124-11.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Tasa Coffee Roasters, 4136 W. North Ave., has been the focus of social media rumors, and on Monday, employees walked out in protest.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Esme Segura, 28, heard about the Tasa allegations and decided to check things out with a friend. </p><p>They arrived with the intention of grabbing some photos and videos of the signs posted by the workers. But once they began recording video of the closed shop, a man inside started tearing down the posters and gestured to a small handgun in his waistband. The video was reviewed by WBEZ/Sun-Times.</p><p>“He just started banging on the door and flicking us off and then he also just flashed his gun or he was pointing at it. He raised his shirt and showed that he had it,” Segura said.</p><p>Police were called to the scene and the man was temporarily detained. Nobody on scene wanted to file a police report, so police released the man after confirming he is legally allowed to carry a firearm, officers at the scene said. The man’s identity has not been confirmed.</p><p>Since Chicago has been an ongoing target of federal immigration enforcement, Segura said it matters to the community if there are ties to the agency carrying out detentions and deportations.</p><p>“It is a Latino space, or they claim it to be a Latino space,” she said. “I feel like, you know, the neighborhood should feel safe going in.”</p><p><i>Contributing: Cam Rodriguez</i></p>

</div><p></p><h3>Mayor Brandon Johnson</h3><p>With a 30% public approval rating and less than $650,000 in his campaign fund, Johnson, 50, is in real danger of becoming Chicago’s second straight one-term mayor. But Johnson has a solid base in the African-American community, and hence a strong chance of making the runoff. He has also delivered on key progressive promises like paid leave, while proposing protections for renters struggling with affordability. But he’s likely to have a much tougher time reaching the 50%-plus-one vote tally he needs to win a second term. The coalition of progressive unions that bankrolled and staffed Johnson’s winning campaign has fractured. The Chicago Teachers Union, where Johnson served as a paid organizer, remains firmly in the mayor’s camp. Wilson's endorsement of Lightfoot sent a signal to his older, church-based constituency that, as he put it, "contracts and jobs and schools" were more important than concerns they may have about Lightfoot being gay. Wilson called his endorsement of Lightfoot "a hell of a mistake." Four years later, he made another political mistake by endorsing Paul Vallas, who lost to Brandon Johnson. Her career veered from nonprofit work into real estate development and property management, where she still works.</p><p>Ma has voiced her support for a universal basic income as a solution to several of the city's key issues and has hailed government programs designed to help immigrants obtain economic and academic opportunities, crediting them with contributing to her own success.</p><h3>Jessica Maronto</h3><p>Maronto, who works for the city repairing traffic signals, devotes a lot of his campaign materials to a pop-up shop style solution to food deserts. The self-described Libertarian has advocated for reducing property taxes by more than 50%, the city declaring bankruptcy over pension payments and repealing Chicago's sanctuary city laws. He also hosts a YouTube-based show called the Meme Podcast.</p>

entries.title: Bulls guard Josh Giddey talks about a new culture of 'accountability'
entries.summary: <p>Accountability remained a buzzword around the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" >Bulls</a> the last few days, specifically in the wake of Josh Giddey and Matas Buzelis getting some tough-love benching late in Friday’s loss to the Wizards.</p><p>Coach Tiago Splitter detailed the reasons more on Sunday, and Giddey has now responded when discussing how he was initially frustrated with the latest decision from his coach but after having a night to absorb it, completely understood where Splitter was coming from.</p><p>“He’s not a guy that will just do that and not talk to you,” Giddey said. “He’s a human. Like he’s really good at communicating and that’s one of the things I respect about him. He can be open and honest about it and we can move forward.”</p><p>They did, and quickly, as Buzelis and Giddey both responded with solid performances against Denver on Sunday, especially Giddey who recorded a triple-double that included a career-high 22 assists.</p><p>So what exactly did Giddey learn in the latest sit-and-watch from his coach?</p><p>“What not to do,” Giddey said. “That’s what got us there in the first place. We have to perform the right way to be out there at the end of games.”</p><p>And while it’s easy to ask why it seems Splitter has focused his tough-love moments on Giddey and Buzelis, the point guard insisted that wasn’t the case. Yes, there is a culture of accountability and it’s being felt by the entire roster.</p><p>“Even during film and things behind the scenes, he’s not going at one or two guys,” Giddey said. “Like everyone on the team is held accountable and that’s the thing as a player you love. And like I said, he’s a former player. He understands you got to hold your best players accountable the same way you hold guys not in the rotation accountable.</p><p>“You look up and down the line, when we go through film and walkthroughs, practices, everyone is held accountable to the same standards. That’s how you get better as a team. We’re doing that, we’re trending in the right direction, and it all starts with that, holding everyone accountable as a coach.”</p><p></p><h3><b>Taking steps</b></h3><h3></h3><p></p><p>It’s easy to forget that there was another first-round pick on the roster not named Caleb Wilson, and maybe that’s because it’s been out of sight, out of mind for Dailyn Swain.</p><p>The No. 15 overall pick has been going back and forth between the big-boy roster and the G League team, but Splitter likes what he's been seeing and hearing about Swain and said there is a plan in place to turn him from project to prospect.</p><p>“First of all, Dailyn is doing a great job in our gym,” Splitter said. “His shot looks so much better, his confidence and energy is so much better. I don’t want to put him on the fire here, we’ve got to be careful when we do it, but slowly he’s going to get more minutes through the season. I’m happy with the work he’s doing with Windy City, and we’ve just got to be patient. It’s a project for us, honestly, and he’s doing great.”</p><p>In the three games he’s played for Windy City he’s averaging 19.7 points, 6.3 rebounds and six assists per game.</p><p></p><h3><b>Answering the bell</b></h3><h3></h3><p></p><p>Nic Claxton didn’t play against the Nuggets because he’s still restricted from back-to-backs after starting off the season nursing a bad hamstring.</p><p>The big did play on Monday, however, despite battling illness and he wasn’t alone. Jalen Smith was also fighting a bug but did his best to try and play through it.</p>

entries.title: Federal appeals court clears way for U.S. Army to detonate degraded bomb-making material in Iowa
entries.summary: <p>A federal appeals court on Monday cleared the way for the U.S. Army to detonate several tons of degraded bomb-making material at an Iowa ammunition plant, finding that the plan should adequately limit the dispersal of lead dust into the atmosphere.</p><p>The order by the 8th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals was one of two decisions President Donald Trump said he was awaiting after he ordered the Army earlier in the day not to detonate the chemicals without court approval. Trump added that the detonation couldn’t go forward unless Gov.-elect Rob Sand also approved. Sand has said the decision is up to the administration.</p><p>In its ruling, the three-judge panel said the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency adequately incorporated safeguards in the emergency permit to minimize the dispersal of dust. Those conditions address the concerns of the environmental groups, the court said.</p><p>The court pointed to the barriers put up around the area where the barrels are stored along with weather restrictions. It also noted the requirements for advance public notification, updated air modeling and environmental monitoring and sampling.</p><p>The judges said the record also reflected that the Army evaluated “a full range” of alternatives, including using other chemicals to neutralize the lead azide and thermal treatment.</p><h3>The blast had been planned for last week</h3><h3></h3><p>The detonation of 68 barrels of lead azide was initially planned for last Friday, but the Army has since changed the date three times following an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects. They had planned for a detonation this coming Wednesday, saying the weather was most favorable that day.</p><p>Environmentalists sued last week to stop the detonation. The court temporarily halted the permit, prompting the Army to argue that it didn’t need authorization after all, given that it was an emergency.</p><p>An attorney for the environmentalists made clear Monday that the legal challenge centers on the validity of the permit, not the Army’s decision to move forward with the detonation under the emergency provision.</p><p>“If they have information that leads them to believe that this is truly an emergency, they should act in the interest of the public,” Rachel Rintelmann, an attorney with Earthjustice, said before the court ruling. She said Trump’s post only added further confusion to what has been a chaotic time for some residents in Iowa.</p><p>“The people of Iowa deserve better than this,” she said.</p><h3>Incoming governor asks why rush to demolition</h3><h3></h3><p>Sand said in a social media post on Sunday that because of previous decisions that have already been made, “No good options exist and the situation is more dangerous and unpredictable than it ever should have been.”</p><p>He questioned why a contract to remove the explosive risk was canceled, why nothing was done and “why we are rushing to demolition now in late November.”</p><p>“The safety of Iowans should be the top priority of everyone involved,” he said. “All relevant federal, state and local government resources should be focused on protecting everyone that could be impacted.”</p><p>Gov. Kim Reynolds activated the state emergency management office on Friday. The state also created a dedicated website for information about the operation.</p><h3>Residents left in limbo as they prepare for detonation</h3><h3></h3><p>Some residents near Middletown, where the ammunition plant is located, have been sealing their windows and doors as a precaution to keep out any lead dust that might result from the detonation. Others who live farther away were raising concern on social media about the possible paths that the plume could take depending on shifts in the wind.</p><p>Officials acknowledge that lead is toxic and have recommended that people stay indoors whenever the detonation happens and clean off outdoor surfaces with water afterwards to limit exposure to any lead particles.</p><p>Middletown Mayor Rodney Johnson said the detonation must take place “so we can move on with our lives.”</p><p>“Improper storage and disposal is where things go wrong,” he said on social media.</p><p>Leaders of states that border Iowa also expressed concern. Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe said authorities don’t believe there will be significant health effects to people and livestock, but state agencies are working to establish additional monitoring of air and water quality, public health and agriculture resources.</p><p>“But I want to emphasize: this is a federal operation,” Kehoe said. “The states of Iowa, Missouri and Illinois do not have a say on when this is conducted. I do join my fellow governors and agency officials in neighboring states in their frustration for how this has been handled.”</p><p>Democratic U.S. Sen. Tammy Baldwin, of Wisconsin, sent Army Secretary Adam Telle a letter Monday expressing “alarm and disapproval” over the handling of the material in Iowa.</p><h3>Army says plans are aimed at avoiding something worse</h3><h3></h3><p>In court filings over the weekend, Army Col. Aaron Teller, a munitions emergency response specialist, explained that less liquid inside the barrels means the solution inside is more susceptible to freezing, which increases the sensitivity of the crystals that have formed around the inside of the rim and underside of the lids.</p><p>“Even a small amount of friction can break the crystal formation, causing an explosive chain reaction,” he said in his declaration to the court.</p><p>In March, staff at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant found several dozen barrels of degraded lead azide, which is used in munitions production. Crystallization of the material created an unstable and dangerous situation, prompting the Army to assemble experts in munitions chemistry, engineering and environmental safety to come up with a plan.</p><p>According to EPA documents, alternatives such as neutralizing and decomposing the drums’ contents with other chemicals were considered. But officials said handling the drums would increase the probability of an accidental, fatal detonation.</p><p>The environmental groups disagreed, arguing in their court filings that other alternatives were not fully considered. They also criticized officials for not sharing more information with the public.</p><p>Officials contend that the risk of an uncontrolled explosion is growing, particularly as temperatures drop. They said there is a risk that the chemicals may explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1 Celsius) in the coming days.</p><h3>Experts say there are no easy answers</h3><h3></h3><p>Lead azide is “very sensitive” and also susceptible to heat, freezing, shock, friction and “all sorts of things that could cause an accidental detonation,” said John Goodpaster, a chemistry professor at Indiana University, Indianapolis. It’s also old, which increases the risk because explosives become increasingly unstable as they age, he said.</p><p>Add in the environmental threat caused by the lead that will escape into the atmosphere and the challenge is significant, Goodpaster said.</p><p>“I do not envy the Army,” Goodpaster said. “They are in a situation where they’ve got a large amount of very dangerous material and not very many good options in terms of trying to dispose of it.”</p><p>But it’s impossible to predict when it could explode on its own, he said.</p><p>“The longer we wait, the longer the risk accumulates that they might have an accidental explosion,” Goodpaster said.</p><p><i>Associated Press writers Scott Bauer in Madison, Wisconsin, and Jacques Billeaud in Phoenix contributed.</i></p>

entries.title: A benching, a showcase by the bench and a win as Bulls beat Cavs
entries.summary: <p>The Bulls don’t need a 22-assist triple-double from guard Josh Giddey every night. But they need him in a place where he can attack the rim, jump-start the attack and make plays in one consistent package.</p><p>So, considering his range of performances in recent games — from a late benching Friday against the Wizards to an impressive recovery Sunday against the Nuggets to another benching Monday against the Cavaliers, how do they get him there?</p><p>“I think he’s a connector, right?” coach Tiago Splitter said. “Like, a guy that can really see the court. For him to be effective and pass the way he passed [Sunday], he’s got to be aggressive. He’s got to bring two guys on him. Every time he’s aggressive and he’s taking care of the ball, something good is going to happen. I keep telling him, ‘Be aggressive. Be you, but be aggressive. Play simple.’ I think that’s the key for him.”</p><p>Giddey has shown those skills this season — just not every time, including in the Bulls’ 122-108 victory Monday at the United Center. His inconsistency got him benched last week in Cleveland and again Friday at the UC before his triple-double in an overtime loss Sunday. He then was benched again Monday with 4:41 left in the fourth quarter and the Bulls leading 113-104. Splitter yanked Giddey and forward Matas Buzelis after a bad turnover on a fast break — Giddey’s third turnover of the game. He finished with 11 assists but only four points and two rebounds.</p><p>“Trying to protect him a little bit,” Splitter said. “Back-to-back [games].”</p><p>Giddey and Buzelis put in heavy minutes Sunday, so the reasoning made sense. But it was obvious neither player was thrilled. Although the Bulls (5-12) were happy to beat the Cavs, more consistent play from Giddey would help answer a long list of questions as the front office pieces together this rebuild.</p><p>“That’s the key for him now: to figure out how to maintain that [high] level and be consistent,” Splitter said. “We need that consistency from him for us to be successful. He’s key for us, and he knows that. He’s got to bring it on both ends. And whenever he plays well, we’re going to have a big game.”</p><p>Giddey’s assists have been largely the same — around 9.3 per game, win or lose. Even his scoring output isn’t dramatically different when the Bulls win or lose this season. But his defense and rebounding are another story, and that’s where the Bulls feel it in the standings. Entering Monday, Giddey was averaging 5.5 rebounds in losses and nine in victories. That’s key, considering it’s Giddey who initiates the offense and its pace when he’s on the court.</p><p>“I think there’s been times throughout the year that I’ve been too unselfish and getting off the ball too soon,” he said. “There’s definitely times I need to be more aggressive and get downhill, and that doesn’t mean to score. Just put pressure on the defense. I think when I get into the paint, guys will collapse, and that’s when I can kick it out, get other guys looks. It’s a matter of finding that balance, and that’s something I’ve got to get better at.”</p><p>That has been an ongoing message from Splitter to both his rookies and his veterans.</p><p>“When you play, sometimes you get to a point where you get lazy,’’ Splitter said. ‘‘You think you are who you are, but there’s always something more out there. There’s always parts of your game where you can get better. I tell these guys all the time, ‘Keep getting better, keep developing.’ Not just the shot, but everything — the defense, the attention to detail. And it’s not linear. It’s up-and-down.’’</p>

entries.title: Former Chicago cop pleads guilty, admits helping smuggle guns to Mexico
entries.summary: <p>A former Chicago police officer pleaded guilty Monday to being involved in a scheme smuggling guns to Mexico after using his police badge to buy them, court records show.</p><p>Kevin Rodriguez, 28, pleaded guilty Monday in U.S. District Court. He now faces up to about eight years in prison at his sentencing hearing Feb. 17.</p><p>Rodriguez was indicted last year on federal felony conspiracy charges stemming from two 2024 gun sales. Diego Valdez, who also was charged, is accused of telling Rodriguez to buy two firearms, including an "AR-style rifle,” which Rodriguez allegedly agreed to purchase using his police department credentials, according to the indictment.</p><p>The two men traveled to Indiana and Rodriguez purchased a rifle, according to the indictment, then a few days later Rodriguez purchased a pistol in Monee, Illinois. A few months later, Valdez brought the guns to Mexico, the indictment says.</p><p>Valdez then allegedly paid Rodriguez more than $2,600 via Zelle around the time of the gun sale. Valdez then smuggled the guns to Mexico with the intent to sell them, according to the indictment. Valdez didn't apply for state permission to possess an assault weapon, according to the indictment. </p><p>Rodriguez's attorney didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.</p><p>Rodriguez was recognized by the Fraternal Order of Police for his role in a 2022 car chase during which he was "impaled on the top of a wrought-iron fence,” and continued chasing a person who ran from a stolen car into an apartment complex in South Chicago. But he was also the subject of several complaints during his time with the police department, including failing to notify the department or file paperwork about a car chase in 2022. He was also accused of verbal abuse and making a traffic stop without probable cause. </p>

entries.title: Brady Pettigrew delivers a late-night show as Bolingbrook knocks off Marshall
entries.summary: <p>Elite high school basketball players sometimes give fans moments they'll remember for years. Flashes of NBA-level speed, power, and athleticism, made even more memorable by the smaller setting. It’s like seeing an arena-level rock band at a small bar.</p><p>That’s why impartial observers were still watching Bolingbrook and Marshall play at midnight on a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-basketball/scores/2026/11/22/chicago-high-school-basketball-scores-illinois" >Monday</a> at St. Xavier’s Shannon Center. And Brady Pettigrew, one of the top 10 players in the national class of 2028 and the guy everyone was there to see, delivered the moment. The 6-5 guard drove through the lane midway through the third quarter and threw down a two-handed dunk over a Marshall defender.</p><p>“They were doubling me this game, and I kinda saw that the person guarding me had slow feet,” Pettigrew said. “I blew past him, and I saw someone under the rim, and it was either he stops [me], or I go through him and finish him. And we all saw how that turned out.”</p><p>Another breakaway dunk immediately followed the standout dunk. Pettigrew scored 20 points in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-basketball/2026/11/20/brady-pettigrew-the-states-biggest-high-school-basketball-star-is-focused-on-a-state-title-for-bolingbrook" >No. 4 Raiders’</a> 66-41 win against Marshall. The two dunks came during a 10-0 Bolingbrook run in which Pettigrew scored eight points.</p><p>“That [dunk] was crazy,” Raiders freshman Layton Jones Jr. said. “The whole crowd went wild.”</p><p>Jones provided his own memorable moment. The highly-regarded freshman finished with 12 points and nine rebounds in his high school debut.</p><p>“I’m super proud of him,” Pettigrew said. “The switch turned on, and you saw him get going. You saw all the hype come true today.”</p><p>Jones, a 6-6 forward, scored in the post, made a three-pointer, and showed impressive court vision while leading fast breaks.</p><p>“I felt comfortable,” entries.title: Dear Abby: Fiance is a great guy, but he and his daughters are slobs
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have been dating a nice man for 18 months. We get along great. He's smart, hardworking, dedicated and loving. We share the same faith. He has been a widower for two years, and I'm divorced.</p><p>When he proposed, I said yes, but I'm worried because his house is always messy and in disarray. He has a big dog that sheds, so there's a lot of fur on the floor. He also tends to leave papers lying around the house. The tub is filthy, and the floors need washing. I love spending time with him, but I get anxious when I think I would have to live like that.</p><p>In addition, his older daughters are slobs, too. He tries to get the girls to help, and he does do some cleaning himself, but it's never really clean. We plan to buy a house of our own, but I'm wondering if I should end the relationship over something that may not be a big deal, or if I'll be miserable as the only one doing housework. Should I overlook this because he's a great guy, or do I break both our hearts and walk away? — <i>TIDY IN CANADA</i></p><p><b>DEAR TIDY:</b> Do not overlook this. If you haven't had a frank discussion with your fiance about household chores, you should. Obviously, your standards of cleanliness differ greatly from his and his daughters' — and probably his late wife's. You should not be stuck in the role of housemaid. If that happens, you will be miserable. Nor should you have to police your home like a white-gloved drill sergeant.</p><p>A monthly cleaning service could fix this problem if the two of you can afford it; so could a firm agreement on their part to cooperate and shape up. Show your fiance what "clean" looks like to you, and demonstrate exactly how much of the burden you are willing to shoulder during a trial month. Do not marry this man until his family can prove they are able to keep their home up to your cleanliness standards.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My husband and I separated almost a year ago. I went on a dating app and met two great guys. One, "Adam," has asked me to marry him, but now I'm back with my husband. Adam refuses to give up on me. The second guy says he will wait until we can be together, which we can't. I'm torn because I love my husband and want things to work out for us, but I have developed feelings for both of these other men. I think both are aware of it. Please advise me. — <i>TOO MUCH CHOICE IN FLORIDA</i></p><p><b>DEAR TOO MUCH:</b> It may seem like you have too much choice, but in reality, you've already made your decision: You never divorced your husband, you still love him and you want your marriage to work. Encouraging the men you have cultivated feelings for during your furlough is unfair to both of them. So quit stalling, pull the plug(s) and get on with your marriage.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: The Thanksgiving we've come to know was created to unite a divided country
entries.summary: <p>It is hard to imagine a more American holiday than Thanksgiving. Every year, elementary schoolers learn about the first celebration: that after surviving a terrible year, New England’s first European immigrants, the Pilgrims, invited their Indigenous neighbors to a feast in gratitude for their help and God’s providence.</p><p>Children learn the story as if it were history — and as though Americans have commemorated Thanksgiving the same way ever since. The only existing <a class="Link" href="https://plimoth.org/yath/unit-4/eye-witness-account-of-the-1621-harvest-celebration" target="_blank" >eyewitness account</a> of this event does not, however, say much about what was eaten. <a class="Link" href="https://plimoth.org/yath/unit-4/excerpt-from-william-bradfords-of-plymouth-plantation-harvest-of-1621" target="_blank" >A slightly later account</a> of the 1621 harvest mentions seasonal food such as venison, corn and, yes, turkeys.</p><p>The idea of a straight line connecting <a class="Link" href="https://theconversation.com/where-are-the-voices-of-indigenous-peoples-in-the-thanksgiving-story-51089" target="_blank" >that “first Thanksgiving</a>” to Thanksgivings today is, in fact, an American myth. It is a story created in the 19th century <a class="Link" href="https://visit.archives.gov/whats-on/explore-exhibits/president-abraham-lincolns-thanksgiving-day-proclamation" target="_blank" >to unify a nation</a> and long used to <a class="Link" href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0308275X9201200205" target="_blank" >assimilate new immigrants</a> into it.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-730000" name="module-730000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>The Pilgrims and Puritans, who started arriving in Massachusetts shortly afterward, <a class="Link" href="https://divinity.uchicago.edu/sightings/articles/thanksgiving-day-remember-fast-day-dean-grodzins" target="_blank" >regularly held fasts and feasts</a>. On fast days, the community atoned for sins they believed they had committed. On feast days, they gave thanks to God. Some governors of colonies — and later, states — <a class="Link" href="https://www.si.edu/spotlight/thanksgiving/history" target="_blank" >declared fall holidays of thanksgiving</a>, but did not coordinate with each other.</p><h3></h3><h3><b>Creating today’s Thanksgiving</b></h3><h3></h3><p>The Thanksgiving that we know, with the traditional recipes and the close connection to the Pilgrims, was largely the creation of one woman: <a class="Link" href="https://www.womenshistory.org/education-resources/biographies/sarah-hale" target="_blank" >Sarah Josepha Hale</a>, who was born in New Hampshire in 1788. In the 1830s she became the editor of <a class="Link" href="https://www.nysoclib.org/blog/special-collections-highlight-godeys-ladys-book-sarah-josepha-hale-and-american-culture" target="_blank" >Godey’s Lady’s Book</a>, which had the largest circulation of any U.S. magazine before the Civil War.</p><p>Godey’s included clothing patterns, recipes, articles on home management, essays on educating children, recipes and fiction. Hale believed that the woman was the heart of the home and responsible for creating an upstanding, God-fearing, wholesome family.</p><p>She was also deeply committed to her young country and believed that homemakers could help create its national identity. According to historian <a class="Link" href="https://history.illinois.edu/directory/profile/epleck" target="_blank" >Elizabeth Pleck</a>, Hale began publishing editorials <a class="Link" href="https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674002791" target="_blank" >calling for a national Thanksgiving</a>, along with instructions for what the day could look like.</p><p>Godey’s taught readers how to celebrate the day, with recipes for seasonal food such as turkey and cranberry sauce. The centerpiece of the table was the pies, which featured elaborate pastry decorations: the Mayflower or a cornucopia, created out of pie crust. The full table was a celebration of “women’s work,” at a time when the Industrial Revolution was <a class="Link" href="https://www.uml.edu/tsongas/barilla-taylor/women-industrial-revolution.aspx" target="_blank" >shifting the<u> </u>economy toward factories and other business</a>, making the importance of unpaid domestic labor less obvious.</p><p>Hale’s idea of Thanksgiving also emphasized returning to loved ones, as those factories were drawing many workers away from home. She saw it as a day to tell family stories — and the story of the nation, starting with the first Thanksgiving.</p><p>Hale <a class="Link" href="https://www.whitehousehistory.org/press-room/press-timelines/thanksgiving-at-the-white-house" target="_blank" >petitioned five presidents</a> to declare Thanksgiving a national holiday. Abraham Lincoln finally took her up on it, hoping that a national holiday emphasizing the country’s origin story would prove uniting during the Civil War.</p><p>Northern women sent pies to the families of soldiers and turkeys to the men at the front. Pleck notes that abolitionist <a class="Link" href="https://www.womenshistory.org/education-resources/biographies/sojourner-truth" target="_blank" >Sojourner Truth</a> <a class="Link" href="https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674002791" target="_blank" >went door to door</a>, collecting funds to provide Thanksgiving dinners to African American troops.</p><p>The holiday <a class="Link" href="https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674002791" target="_blank" >caught on gradually</a>. Given the Protestant origins of early Americans’ feast and fast days, Catholics were slow to embrace it. Given its association with Lincoln and the war, the South was also late to adopt it. And given the day’s emphasis on family, it was less celebrated on the frontier, where single men dominated.</p><p>Wherever Thanksgiving was celebrated, however, Godey’s Lady’s Book taught Americans how to celebrate it. The magazine’s op-eds connected the holiday menu and the past, using the Pilgrims’ courage to inspire 19th-century Americans dealing with massive changes in their own lives: war, industrialization, urbanization and the frontier.</p><h3>Assimilating immigrants</h3><p>Before long, Thanksgiving was also seen as a way to assimilate immigrants.</p><p>This vision was, in part, popularized by political cartoonist <a class="Link" href="https://www.illustrationhistory.org/artists/thomas-nast" target="_blank" >Thomas Nast</a>. “<a class="Link" href="https://www.nyhistory.org/blogs/uncle-sams-thanksgiving-dinner-thomas-nasts-powerful" target="_blank" >Uncle Sam’s Thanksgiving Dinner</a>,” which appeared in Harper’s Weekly in 1869, depicting Americans from any number of races and ethnicities in their national dress: men, women and children sitting as equals around a dinner table, with portraits of presidents on the wall, while Uncle Sam carved a turkey.</p><p>The image suggested that immigrants could be incorporated into the nation — and formerly enslaved people, too. It was printed just one year after <a class="Link" href="https://constitution.congress.gov/constitution/amendment-14/" target="_blank" >the 14th Amendment</a> granted citizenship to anyone born in the U.S. and four years after the <a class="Link" href="https://constitution.congress.gov/constitution/amendment-13/" target="_blank" >13th Amendment</a> formally ended slavery.</p><p>Nast’s image contrasted sharply to another cartoon, also called “<a class="Link" href="https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Uncle-Sams-Thanksgiving-Dinner-by-George-Frederick-Keller_fig1_313536819" target="_blank" >Uncle Sam’s Thanksgiving Dinner</a>,” that G.F. Keller drew for the San Francisco Wasp eight years later. Keller’s disheveled and entirely male collection of diners each ate their own national food, or offensive stereotypes thereof, suggesting immigrants could never truly become American.</p><p>But Many Americans believed they could — although they demanded most immigrants give up their “Old World ways” and take on customs of their new country. Thanksgiving was part of the engine of that assimilation.</p><p>In the early 20th century, public schools taught about Thanksgiving and sent children home with recipe cards so that their parents could cook the same kinds of recipes Hale had popularized in the previous century. Schools framed the Pilgrims and their first Thanksgiving as the spiritual, if not literal, ancestors of all Americans: the first “immigrants.” They didn’t dwell on how the Pilgrims’ arrival <a class="Link" href="https://theconversation.com/thanksgiving-stories-gloss-over-the-history-of-us-settlement-on-native-lands-213517" target="_blank" >looked more like colonization</a> than immigration.</p><p>The holiday became a way to include newcomers in the national myth. By the 1920s, in fact, Thanksgiving was <a class="Link" href="https://time.com/5725168/thanksgiving-history-lesson/" target="_blank" >the most celebrated holiday</a> <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/roomfordebate/2015/11/25/rethinking-the-way-we-teach-thanksgiving/does-thanksgiving-even-belong-in-schools" target="_blank" >in public schools</a>. Pleck quotes one Jewish immigrant reflecting on his childhood and saying the Pilgrims were a way to connect “us offspring of Jewish immigrants — our own exiled fathers who had crossed the seas — <a class="Link" href="https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674002791" target="_blank" >and the traditions of Protestant America</a>.” Students acted out the first Thanksgiving and were told they belonged to a “nation of immigrants.”</p><p>While some immigrant parents rejected the holiday, others embraced it, with spins to make it their own. Many served a turkey surrounded by the celebratory dishes of their own cultures. For Jews, the early 1900s <a class="Link" href="https://mjhnyc.org/blog/crisco-and-the-jewish-american-cook/" target="_blank" >invention of Crisco</a> <a class="Link" href="https://theconversation.com/how-crisco-toppled-lard-and-made-americans-believers-in-industrial-food-127158" target="_blank" >as a nondairy butter substitute</a> allowed them to create a truly “American” Thanksgiving and dessert, without violating kosher rules against mixing meat and milk.</p><p>The fact that most families celebrate at home allowed immigrants and their children to take part in the national culture, while still expressing their own. During my own New England childhood, an Indian neighbor had my mother’s fairly classic cranberry relish, and by the end of the weekend she’d worked transformed it into a cranberry chutney with Indian spices. When we had Thankgiving dinner with my parents’ friends the Stalzmans, who were Jewish, matzo ball soup was the opening course.</p><p>At times, the idea of the Pilgrims arriving on the Mayflower <a class="Link" href="https://www.axios.com/2024/11/27/first-thanksgiving-history-pilgrims" target="_blank" >has been used to exclude</a> — to imply that only Americans <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/1985/09/05/mayflower-descendants-a-breed-apart/" target="_blank" >whose literal ancestors came over on the ship</a>, and other white Protestants like them, truly belong. Yet on the holiday in their memory, generations of new Americans affirmed that they, too, belonged.</p><p><i>Samira Mehta is a professor of women and gender studies and Jewish studies at the University of Colorado Boulder.  </i></p><p><i>This article first appeared on </i><a class="Link" href="https://theconversation.com/us" target="_blank" ><i><u>The Conversation</u></i></a><i>, a nonprofit news site dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scientists.</i></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-0a0000" name="html-embed-module-0a0000"></a><iframe src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/289016/count.gif?distributor=republish-lightbox-advanced" width="1" height="1" style="border: none !important" referrerpolicy="no-referrer-when-downgrade"></iframe> </div> </div><p></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-1b0000" name="module-1b0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Too afraid to tax the rich, many Democrats OK with taxing the poor’s gambling losses
entries.summary: <p>Afraid or unwilling to tax the gains of the rich, politicians are making it easier for working people to lose what they have. Then they’re taxing that.</p><p>Online casinos are the newest example. Slots and blackjack on every phone, around the clock. Eight states have legalized them. Now Washington, D.C., may be next.</p><p>On Nov. 18, a D.C. Council committee <a class="Link" href="https://www.dcnewsnow.com/news/local-news/washington-dc/dc-council-committee-advances-bill-to-legalize-online-casino-gambling/" target="_blank" >advanced online casinos</a> 3–1, projecting $73 million over four years. Three Democrats voted yes. The only no came from independent Councilwoman Christina Henderson.</p><p>“I don’t think we can build our revenue on the backs of people’s addictions,” she said.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-520000" name="module-520000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>It took an independent to say it.</p><p>The council’s racial equity office warned that online casinos could harm Black residents and other residents of color who gamble. More than nine out of 10 Washingtonians living in poverty are people of color.</p><p>Poor white families face that danger, too. Nationally, non-Hispanic white Americans account for more than four in 10 people in poverty — the largest single racial or ethnic group.</p><p>As Martin Luther King Jr. wrote from a Birmingham jail, “We are caught in an inescapable network of mutuality, tied in a single garment of destiny.”</p><p>I came into the Democratic Party as president of Youth for Jackson ’88 in my county. Years later, I traveled around Washington with former Mayor Marion Barry as a young volunteer on a write-in mayoral campaign for the Rev. Willie Wilson, a pastor from Ward 8, the city’s poorest ward.</p><p>Whatever you think you know about Barry, ordinary people loved him for a reason. I saw why.</p><p>He made sure seniors had decent, affordable housing. He helped young people find jobs by the thousands. He believed government should make it easier for people who worked hard to build better lives.</p><p>Now Democrats in his city want to put a casino in every pocket.</p><p>For all its failures, the Democratic Party promised that America is stronger when working people prosper. Andrew Jackson’s version excluded Black Americans.</p><p>Generations expanded that promise, from Franklin Roosevelt and Lyndon Johnson to the Rev. Jesse Jackson’s Rainbow Coalition.</p><p>The promise was never that the rich couldn’t get richer. It was that the rest of us would, too.</p><p>Consider Illinois. In fiscal 2026, the state collected <a class="Link" href="https://news.wttw.com/2026/10/08/illinois-tax-revenue-gambling-increased-19-last-year-report-finds" target="_blank" >$2.7 billion in gambling-related taxes</a>, up 19% in a year. Bettors lost nearly $1.4 billion on online sports betting alone. Now legislators want to add online casinos.</p><p>Illinois resident Dane Miller alleges DraftKings encouraged his addiction as he wagered more than $2 million. He says he gambled away his wedding savings, borrowed against his retirement, lost his job and eventually wrote a suicide note. Those allegations concern sports betting, not online casinos, and remain unproven. But how much misery are lawmakers prepared to risk for more revenue?</p><p>Follow the money.</p><p>Sportsbooks steered more than $20 million into a Democratic-aligned political fund. It spent over<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/03/18/illinois-primary-super-pac-spending-aipac-cryptocurrency-ai-sports-betting" > $2.5 million </a>in Chicago-area Democratic legislative primaries. In D.C., it spent $417,000 on Council election mailers promoting three Democrats and an independent. Democratic Councilman Zachary Parker, a beneficiary, voted to advance online casinos.</p><p>The mailers didn’t mention gambling.</p><p>Supporters say legalization would regulate underground gambling and fund services. But raising tax revenue this way depends on making it easier for gamblers to lose money — and harder for those struggling to stop.</p><p>Legalization doesn’t simply regulate an existing market. It brings advertising, bonuses and recruitment campaigns. Casinos once reserved personal attention for high rollers. Software can now track gamblers bet by bet, tailoring offers to bring them back. A physical casino has doors you can walk out of. This one follows you home.</p><p>A factory creates something of value. Even a casino resort creates hotel and restaurant jobs. An online casino can drain a neighborhood without opening a door there.</p><p>In Maryland’s 2024 House vote on online casinos, 35 Republicans and just eight Democrats voted no. The bill passed before dying in the Senate.</p><p>I think about Marion Barry and the families he worked so hard to help. He didn’t help lift families out of poverty so government could profit by making them easy prey for casinos in their pockets.</p><p>From Springfield to Washington, my fellow Democrats need to remember whose side we’re supposed to be on.</p><p>I can still hear Jesse Jackson asking, “Why should the poor pay more?”</p><p><i>Ben Jealous is a professor of practice at the University of Pennsylvania and former president and CEO of the NAACP.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ce0000" name="module-ce0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Traveling for Thanksgiving? Here are some air travel tips as 2 million expected at O'Hare and Midway
entries.summary: <p>The week of Thanksgiving is a historically busy time for travel, and recent disruptions to flights have some Chicagoans on edge.</p><p>The Chicago Department of Aviation estimates 2 million people will make their way through Chicago's airports this week, an increase from last year even as national estimates <a class="Link" href="https://newsroom.aaa.com/2026/11/aaa-thanksgiving-holiday-travel-forecast/" target="_blank" >dipped a bit</a>, according to AAA. Around 1.67 million people are expected to come through O'Hare International Airport, 7.2% more than the seven-day period around Thanksgiving last year. At Midway International Airport, more than 353,000 people are expected to pass through, 2% more than last year, according to the aviation department.</p><p>"“At O’Hare and Midway, we are fortunate each Thanksgiving season to host travelers who are eagerly awaiting the chance to see loved ones again,” CDA Commissioner Mike McMurray said in a news release. “It is a top priority that we set the tone for their holiday travels with outstanding service and hospitality, and we can’t wait to make them feel at home like they are friends and family.”</p><p>If you're navigating a busy airport this week, here are some tips to keep in mind.</p><h3>Arrive early</h3><p>Lines at security may be long at either airport, and the Transportation Security Administration and U.S. Customs and Border Protection advise building extra time into your schedule. If you have CLEAR or TSA Pre-Check, that could help you get through security faster, but it's not a guarantee and you should still try to arrive early.</p><p>If you have time to kill after entering the terminal, both O'Hare and Midway have artists and other entertainers scheduled throughout the week. See the schedule at <a class="Link" href="https://www.flychicago.com/" target="_blank" >flychicago.com</a>.</p><h3>Avoid clogging the pick-up and drop-off areas</h3><p>If you're driving someone to or from the airport, it's important to wait to pull up to the doors until they're ready, the CDA said. Circling the terminals causes unnecessary traffic and more of a headache for yourself and other drivers.</p><p>Instead, use the cellphone lots, where you can wait nearby until you're ready to go. At O'Hare, the cellphone lot is at 560 N. Bessie Coleman Drive. Midway's is at 61st Street and Cicero Avenue, just south of the airport.</p><p>Another option is the Kiss n' Fly at both airports, where travelers can make their way to the airport without a car. At O'Hare, passengers can be dropped off at the Multi-Modal Facility, 10255 W. Zemke Blvd., and board the Airport Transit System for a quick ride to all terminals. At Midway, passengers can walk from the Kiss n' Fly, located at 59th Street and Kilpatrick Avenue.</p><p>The CDA also recommends using the CTA, Metra or Pace to get to and from both airports.</p><h3>Be a respectful traveler</h3><p>Tom Stuker has flown nearly 24 million miles and is believed to be the world's most frequent flyer. He has some travel etiquette tips for fellow flyers, and most of them have to do with common courtesy.</p><p>"Don't get on a phone and talk 'blah-blah-blah' about business for 30 minutes when you could text them or email them," he said in a <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/Cu2ziacpKpl/" target="_blank" >video</a> posted on Instagram. "I don't want to go to your sales meeting."</p><p>He also discouraged people from stealing things off the plane, saying that behavior could contribute to the rising price of airfare. </p><p>Stuker also wishes people wouldn't take out their frustrations on airline staff.</p><p>"When the weather's bad and it delays or cancels the flight, don't start screaming at the airline," he said. "If you have a problem, take it up with God, he's the one that brought the storms on."</p>

entries.title: Da Brat is ready to remind Chicago of her place in music history
entries.summary: <p>Some people know Da Brat as the first female solo rapper to go platinum, opening the door for performers such as Nicki Minaj and Cardi B.</p><p>Others know her in her more recent roles: as a radio co-host on “The Rickey Smiley Morning Show,” or as an inspiring figure in the LGBTQ+ community after coming out publicly in 2020 and marrying her wife, Jesseca "Judy" Harris-Dupart, in 2022. But she said she was taken aback by the crowd’s excitement during her performance this year at "The Dinah,” a Palm Springs festival celebrating queer women.</p><div class="Enhancement FormEnhancement" Randolph St.<br><b>When:</b> Nov. 24-29<br><b>Info:</b> Tickets are $52.85-$187.30; <a class="Link" href="http://broadwayinchicago.com" target="_blank" >broadwayinchicago.com</a></div> </div><p>Da Brat also performed at the show’s stops in Washington, D.C. She said Chicago audiences can expect her to hype up the crowd and rap some of her “iconic verses.” While she doesn’t have a signature holiday song to contribute to the show<b> </b>– the festive tunes she recorded over the years with her queen-of-Christmas bestie Mariah Carey and fellow hometown hero Jennifer Hudson are unreleased – Da Brat is confident she can still fill the crowd with cheer.</p><p>“I just hope people enjoy something fresh and fun for the holiday season because the world is a mess right now,” she said. “We need to laugh. We need to enjoy ourselves.”</p><p>“The Nutcracker” wasn’t among the productions Da Brat attended with her family during her youth in the Austin neighborhood.</p><p>“My grandmother was saved and sanctified and filled with the Holy Ghost,” she said. “There was no ‘Nutcracker.’ It was the rapture play or an Easter play or a Christmas play at church with Jesus hanging on the cross.”</p><p>When she wasn’t at Christ Temple Apostolic Faith Church on South Ashland Avenue, she was hitting up her favorite neighborhood businesses, from White Castle and Peeples Taco to sneaker shops and Uncle Remus on Madison Street. Or she was riding her scooter to the South Side after school to rehearse with her girl group, <a class="Link" href="https://www.facebook.com/sosobrat/photos/haaaa-i-use-to-be-in-a-group-called-simply-nasty-in-chicago-we-wore-cat-suits-wi/1967773810017073/" target="_blank" ><u>Simply Nasty</u></a>.</p><p>When it came to Chicago hip-hop acts, Da Brat said she looked up to Da Smart, Crucial Conflict, Prince Akeem and Twista, who inspired her rapid-fire rhymes.</p><p>“Nobody could rap as fast as him,” she said. “It was a challenge for us to be able to keep up. I studied all of his albums.”</p><p>Da Brat credits her godmother and other loved ones, including half-sister and actress LisaRaye McCoy, with introducing her to industry contacts. She got her big break in 1992 after winning a rap contest at a <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/1992/10/04/kris-kross-upbeat-cool/" target="_blank" ><u>Kris Kross concert</u></a> at the Arie Crown Theater. entries.title: Review: Northlight Theatre’s ‘All the World’ will make you fall in love with rom-coms again
entries.summary: <p>Ah, the rom-com. A genre that has fallen out of fashion. Tom Hanks and Meg Ryan are senior citizens. Newer pop culture romances often involve at least one supernatural creature. To the jaded, irony-doused consumer of antiheroes and grit, the rom-com can look hokey, formulaic and mossbacked.</p><p>That attitude, however, is no fun. The romantic comedy, for all its predictability, can be delightful in the right hands, when you like the couple and can genuinely root for them to overcome the obstacles the fates have placed in their way, and when the comedy is truly funny.</p><p>That’s how it is in Lauren Gunderson’s world premiere play, “All the World,” running at the new Northlight Theatre building in downtown Evanston through Dec. 20. Gunderson has strung together a story of the course of true love not running smoothly, as it never does, proceeding inexorably to a happy ending, with ample laughter along the way.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-060000" name="module-060000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>When:</b> Through Dec. 20<br><b>Where:</b> Northlight Theatre, 1012 Church St., Evanston<br><b>Tickets:</b> $36+<br>Info: <a class="Link" href="https://northlight.org/series/all-the-world/" target="_blank" >northlight.org</a><br><b>Run time:</b> One hour, 45 minutes, with one intermission</div> </div><p>Our star-crossed lovers are Ros (Alejandra Escalante) and Jake (Ryan Hallahan), two actors whose relationship plays out in a theater’s green room over a series of shows they appear in together. It begins with Jake arriving backstage to find Ros dancing alone to Daddy Yankee’s “Gasolina,” doing her pre-show warm-up routine. Of course, this charmingly embarrasses them both.</p><p>Jake has been called in as the understudy for Bob Cratchit in “A Christmas Carol,” after the original Bob suffered an injury that, as Jake says, would mean having two Cratchits on crutches. Ros is Mrs. Cratchit. She runs through dance steps with him and reminds him that he needs to know all the words to “Good King Wenceslas,” and the romantic seeds are planted.</p><p>The backstage setting, with two characters steeped in theater, gives Gunderson an opening to pepper the script with knowing references and quotations from other plays, cleverly written with a tone of shared joke rather than in-joke. When Ros and Jake talk about context-free Shakespeare quotations on coffee mugs and tea towels, you know Gunderson has a whole speech she could deliver. The deep marination in this world makes “All the World” the kind of play that invariably gets sold as “a love letter to the theater,” if that weren’t a bit too on the nose for a romantic comedy.</p><p>And so Ros and Jake proceed beyond “A Christmas Carol” through “As You Like It,” an adaptation of “Pride and Prejudice,” “Much Ado About Nothing” and “Our Town.” (The inclusion of “Pride and Prejudice” also winks toward Gunderson’s several Christmas at Pemberley shows she did with Northlight.) The chief pre-intermission obstacle to their love is Ros’ insistence that offstage entanglements could affect the work onstage, a don’t-fish-off-the-company-pier principle.</p><div class="Enhancement" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Alejandra Escalante and Ryan Hallahan star in “All the World” at Northlight Theatre. The early obstacle to their love is Ros’ insistence that offstage entanglements could affect the work onstage, a don’t-fish-off-the-company-pier principle.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Michael Brosilow</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>In the second half, things get loused up by an out-of-the-blue text message from Jake’s past. Unlike most of the other side aspects of the story, where Gunderson prepares later developments carefully, this obstacle for Ros and Jake feels artificial. It doesn’t help matters that “All the World” is a two-hander, so we never see the texter’s in-person effect on Jake, but only how he speaks about it to Ros or grabs for his phone when it dings.</p><p>Gunderson has created a tricky problem for herself by having the story reach a point of resolution at the end of both halves of the show. Another show with this structure (and another show with meta-theatrical elements), “The Fantasticks,” at least hints at troubles to come and then in the second half, makes the audience reassess the first half and its similar arc.</p><p>It’s a small quibble, though, for a show that keeps you smiling throughout. Both actors have great comedic delivery — exceeding expectations even when they are set high by the characters talking about good acting — and convincingly inhabited characters. Escalante, in particular, conveys the somewhat busy, somewhat anxious energy of a familiar type of theater person.</p><p>And the real breath of minty fresh air is to see the romantic comedy revived, with all its winning sparkle. Not the Hallmark movie type, not the alt-y manic pixie dream girl type and not the mopey disaffected-college-graduate type. The fizzy, flirty, funny type that we haven’t seen new material in for a while.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a entries.title: Illinois legislation could help more survivors of campus sexual assault stay in college
entries.summary: <p>Northwestern University senior Erika Ruiz-Yamamoto nearly dropped out of school two years ago after reporting her sexual assault to college officials.</p><p>The aspiring doctor struggled to process what happened to her while juggling intense classes in what’s known as a “weed-out year” for premedical students. She requested basic accommodations for her schoolwork, like more time to complete assignments.</p><p>But Ruiz-Yamamoto said professors and administrators repeatedly denied her requests because they didn’t want to set a precedent for other students. She had to take a biology exam two days after she was assaulted.</p><p>“It felt like it was a constant situation of me having to demonstrate or convince or put on a show of just how badly I needed their assistance or their empathy,” Ruiz-Yamamoto said. “My sexual assault rocked my entire academic experience.”</p><p>A spokesperson for Northwestern did not respond to a request for comment, but according to its policy, the university will offer and provide survivors with reasonable accommodations, like help changing their class schedules.</p><p>Across the country, 1 in 3 survivors of sexual violence drop out of college, according to <a class="Link" href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9660281/" target="_blank" ><u>national research</u></a> — slightly higher than the overall dropout rate. First-year students who experience sexual violence are even more likely to leave school.</p><p>Illinois is one of a handful of states with a law aimed at stopping that. The <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/Legislation/ILCS/Articles?ActID=3672&ChapterID=18&Chapter=HIGHER%20EDUCATION&MajorTopic=EDUCATION" target="_blank" ><u>Preventing Sexual Violence in Higher Education Act</u></a> requires public and private campuses to provide survivors with reasonable supports that can enable them stay in school, like help getting extensions or counseling. It was enacted in 2015.</p><p>But advocates for those who have experienced campus sexual assault say many Illinois colleges are still not doing enough to help survivors like Ruiz-Yamamoto — and they want real consequences for colleges that neglect these obligations.</p><p>“Right now, if you don’t do what's required by the law, there's almost nothing the survivor can do to enforce the law,” said Sarah Beuning, an attorney for the Illinois Coalition Against Sexual Assault, which runs nonprofit rape crisis centers across the state. “If you want to stay and it's your dream and it's your goal, I feel like we should be supporting that as much as possible.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus/FullText?GAID=18&DocNum=4990&DocTypeID=HB&LegId=0&SessionID=114" target="_blank" ><u>State lawmakers are considering a bill</u></a> that would allow college students who’ve been sexually assaulted to sue their institutions if they show “deliberate indifference” to a survivor’s request for support. The proposal would also require universities to provide support or appropriate alternatives regardless of what a student is studying.</p><p>“We've heard from students who've had to drop out of classes because the perpetrator was going to be in their class,” Beuning said. That can push back a survivor’s graduation date and make them pay more in tuition.</p><p>“I understand there are some classes that are offered once a semester with one professor in one room, and that's really hard,” Beuning said. But “we would like universities to try really hard to come up with an alternative support that keeps their student on track and lets them still have a full experience as a college student.”</p><p>The bill has support from Republican and Democratic state lawmakers and proponents are hopeful it will pass during the December veto session. But the legislation has faced opposition from public and private universities across Illinois, including Northwestern University.</p><p>Ruiz-Yamamoto said she’s grateful advocates are focusing on survivors and what they need to stay in school, but also disappointed some universities won't do more without the threat of being sued.</p><p>“Besides the time, it takes a lot of money to stand up to these powerful institutions and individuals that really do play a role in your future career,” she said.</p><p>But for Ruiz-Yamamoto, who is on track to graduate in the spring with a double major in biology and global health, speaking out will be worth it if it means other students get the support she did not.</p><p><i>Lisa Kurian Philip covers higher education for WBEZ in partnership with </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.opencampusmedia.org/" target="_blank" ><i><u>Open Campus</u></i></a><i>.</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/11/09/university-of-chicago-rarely-expels-students-found-responsible-for-sexual-assault-records-show" >UChicago rarely expels students found responsible for sexual assault, records show</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/10/21/students-reflect-on-the-issue-of-campus-sexual-assault-at-uchicago" >UChicago students, high school senior reflect on issue of campus sexual assault</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/14/university-of-chicago-assault-puts-fraternity-safety-problems-in-the-spotlight" >University of Chicago reported assault puts fraternity safety problems in spotlight</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Where to eat Puerto Rican food in Chicago
entries.summary: <p>I was born in Humboldt Park and spent several memorable years of my childhood there. But in the early 2000s, Chicago looked different. My dad, who’d survived complicated family dynamics and chaos in Puerto Rico, New York City and finally Chicago, was ready for a change.</p><p>We ended up in rural Illinois. But in the (back-then) naughts of Oswego, finding food made by our own people was impossible. And my mom wasn’t going to spend hours in the kitchen making pasteles and alcapurria when she had to commute for her job in Downtown Chicago. We kept making trips back to reliable places such as Papa’s Cache Saboroso or Nellie’s Restaurant on Division Street, or Paseo Boricua. In high school, gourmet Caribbean staples like chef Yari Vargas’ Casa Yari popped up in the city. Restaurants like hers made me want to move back for college.</p><p>Whenever my dad would check on me between classes, he’d ask if I’d eaten. The answer was almost always no. We’d often try a new restaurant or cuisine, but some of my favorite meals were at Puerto Rican restaurants helmed by authentic, independent chefs and their families.</p><p>Now, in my job as a reporter, I’m often asked by colleagues, sources, friends and acquaintances for my picks. Though we couldn’t cover everything, these six old-school and new-school restaurants are worth visiting for anyone whose knowledge of Puerto Rican food is limited to the jibarito.</p><h3><b>Borinquen, 3811 N. Western Ave. in North Center.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>My editor and colleague Dorothy Hernandez, photographer Anthony Vazquez and I stopped at <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/borinquen_jibarito/?hl=en" target="_blank" ><u>Borinquen</u></a> in Roscoe Village for lunch on a recent weekday. The original restaurant was in Humboldt Park at 1720 N. California Ave., and it is where the famous jibarito was “invented” by the original owner, Juan “Peter” Figueroa. Today, his niece Gaby Figueroa helps run the new eatery with her father. That day, she greeted us at the counter. “Plantain sandwiches are not a new thing,” she told us. And she’s right: using flattened and fried plantains to replace sandwich bread is nothing new on the island. Today, matriarch Zoraida Rivera, wife of owner Roberto Tañon, helps keep day-to-day operations running smoothly. The best time to eat at <a class="Link" href="https://www.facebook.com/labruquena.chicago/" target="_blank" ><u>La Bruquena</u></a> is on a Friday or Saturday night, when the restaurant hosts live Latin music, including salsa and bomba. Here, Rivera gave us a lesson on pique. Puerto Rican cuisine is not typically spicy. But some people (myself and Dorothy included) like to kick things up a notch. The uniquely Puerto Rican pique is a spicy vinegar-based sauce typically infused with hot ají or chile peppers, herbs and garlic. At La Bruquena, Rivera makes her own in a large, repurposed bottle of rum that travels from table to table.</p><p><b>We tried: </b>The frituras (fried foods) platter that included alcapurrias, Caribbean food, I will suggest Casa Yari. While this place is a recent addition to Paseo Boricua, chef and owner Yari Vargas has deep ties to Chicago’s Puerto Rican community. After more than a decade at her Logan Square eatery on Fullerton Avenue, Vargas was forced to close her restaurant after the landlord sold the building last spring. But in February, she ended up on Division Street in the former space of Latin American Restaurant, one of the block’s first Latin restaurants. Patrons fill the restaurant nightly, craving Vargas’ nostalgia-fueled and upscale dishes based on recipes from her childhood in Chicago with a Puerto Rican mother and Honduran father. Casa Yari is also BYOB, so head across the street to Yauco Liquors for some premium rum to pair with your nonalcoholic passion fruit Moscow Mule or coconut mojito.</p><p><b>We tried: </b>Yari’s famous pastelón, which includes sun-dried tomato jam and picadillo, or ground beef<b> </b>seasoned with tomato and onion. The entree is a take on a popular sweet-and-savory layered plantain dish from Puerto Rico, sort of like a lasagna.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" If everyone wants to try or re-experience Chicago Puerto Rican food, I typically suggest <a class="Link" href="https://www.google.com/aclk?sa=L&pf=1&ai=DChsSEwj-4KuB8_GXAxUqh8IIHZXlChgYACICCAEQABoCamY&co=1&ase=2&gclid=Cj0KCQiA77DXBhCHARIsAHf2MNq8dSnWO_mfCLp9jFAx6m5SLL4jcyd2uLSeKx6f0685vtRQVzIHAuQaArM_EALw_wcB&cid=CAASWuRo0cclSL_XRZsgi1bJdAW7wt6HnEvpkHRO-pKr9a7zuxxRDAZBUaAa2-b0WFA8e_Gg5e271NLKAHA8aHyJko7SPbZOIIjhHfiAir1nZafnwYfn4Mgoye-1sA&cce=2&category=acrcp_v1_32&sig=AOD64_2mWgfrx7YuACi-LF6VdPSteX2jew&q&nis=4&adurl=https://www.jibaritoschicago.com/?gad_source%3D1%26gad_campaignid%3D22982788050%26gbraid%3D0AAAABBUvbWJdGmqCMFrbxyz36zqnE_xgv%26gclid%3DCj0KCQiA77DXBhCHARIsAHf2MNq8dSnWO_mfCLp9jFAx6m5SLL4jcyd2uLSeKx6f0685vtRQVzIHAuQaArM_EALw_wcB&ved=2ahUKEwiOy6aB8_GXAxVjNYYAHVORMwMQ0Qx6BAhXEAs" target="_blank" ><u>Jibaritos on Harlem</u></a> because the drive isn’t too long and the dishes taste like they’re from my Ñaña’s kitchen. Besides solid dishes like mofongo, bistec encebollado and (of course) the jibarito, this spot also has a great brunch menu with Puerto Rican-inspired dishes such as guava pancakes, tostón toast — think avocado toast — and the jibarito breakfast burger. This is also a great place to add to your chinchorreo lineup. (That is, a night of bar hopping and eating with your best buds, great music and endless Medalla Lights.) The concept will <b>move</b> right next to the historic Green Mill at 4804 N. Broadway in Uptown. Chef Roldán has an item I have never seen on any Puerto Rican restaurant menu before: gandul hummus. At <a class="Link" href="https://marinasbistrochicago.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Marina’s</u></a>, pigeon peas (gandules) are transformed into a creamy dip served with plantain chips. That creativity, especially from a chef who has lived and worked in Puerto Rico’s fine dining scene, makes it worthy of a whole-evening dinner experience. He made history in 2025 as the first and only Puerto Rican to ever participate in the city-sponsored culinary event <a class="Link" href="https://www.choosechicago.com/articles/festivals-special-events/chicago-gourmet/" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago Gourmet</u></a>. The tabletops are covered with collages of family photos from different eras of owner Victor García’s family and life in Chicago. One wall features autographs from famous Puerto Ricans who’ve dined at the restaurant over the years, like actor Luis Gúzman or <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2024/05/15/liza-colon-zayas-connects-with-her-inner-child-in-john-krasinski-film-if" target="_blank" ><u>Liza Colón-Zayas</u></a>, best known as Tina on FX’s “The Bear.” Even Guy Fieri has co-signed on this iconic spot. Opened in 2002, this generational family-run restaurant is best known for its “pollochón,” or rotisserie-style chicken marinated in a house adobo or sazón reminiscent of Puerto Rican lechón, or slow-roasted pork. García said his recipe is his late brother’s, and while it’s a treasured family secret, it includes the basics of a good adobo: herbs, garlic and achiote. The cozy dining room is a welcome wintertime escape, but its large outdoor patio is perfect for summer afternoons soaking up the Division Street scene.</p><p><b>We tried: </b>The rib-eye steak jibarito with arroz con gandules.
