entries.title: Microschooling has grown in Illinois. Here’s what it's like for one Chicago teacher and south suburban mom
entries.summary: <p>A couple years ago, Ollie Allen had offers for two full-time teaching positions sitting on her desk.</p><p>She’d spent time substitute teaching at two public elementary schools in Chicago, one run by the district and the other by a charter network. At both, she was known for her ability to ease challenging behavior and work with students who need one-on-one support.</p><p>But Allen made the daring decision to decline both offers and instead open up her own “microschool” — an education model outside of traditional school systems that’s <a class="Link" href="https://stateline.org/2025/08/08/microschools-are-growing-in-popularity-but-state-regulations-havent-caught-up/" target="_blank" ><u>growing across the country</u></a>.</p><p>“I felt like too many kids were being left behind,” Allen said of the schools where she’d worked.</p><p>Microschooling took off in the early days of the pandemic, when schools offered little or no in-person instruction and parents went in search of other options for their children. <a class="Link" href="https://www.usnews.com/education/k12/articles/what-is-a-microschool" target="_blank" ><u>The model has persisted</u></a>, and researchers estimate that nationally, between 1 and 2 million school-age children are enrolled in microschools, <a class="Link" href="https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA3698-1.html" target="_blank" ><u>according to a 2025 report</u></a> from the RAND Corporation, a nonprofit research organization. That’s on par with the number of students enrolled in K-12 Catholic schools.</p><p>Though there’s no standard definition of a microschool, these programs tend to be small, with around 15 students or less. They typically include multiple grades in the same class and offer lessons that cater to individual students’ interests and learning styles, as opposed to standardized curricula. Microschools often charge tuition and can operate as private schools, homeschools or private businesses.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Microschools tend to be small and include students at different grade levels. They can offer students the chance to learn lessons tailored to their interests and needs, but in Illinois they often operate as homeschools with little state oversight.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Kameron Clepper/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The size of the movement varies widely, depending on factors like state legislation and private school regulations, according to Don Soifer of the National Microschooling Center. Microschools have exploded in popularity in states like Florida and Arizona, where school choice programs <a class="Link" href="https://www.fldoe.org/schools/school-choice/k-12-scholarship-programs/ftc/pep-faqs.stml" target="_blank" ><u>have expanded</u></a> in recent years and <a class="Link" href="https://www.azed.gov/esa" target="_blank" ><u>now allow families</u></a> to put state scholarship funds toward microschool tuition.</p><p>The microschooling movement exists but isn’t as robust in Illinois, a state with strict private school regulations and more limited school choice programs, says Soifer.</p><p>It’s unclear how many microschools exist in Illinois. Many operate as homeschools with no state oversight and <a class="Link" href="https://www.isbe.net/Pages/Homeschool.aspx" target="_blank" ><u>few requirements</u></a> — namely that they must teach six key subjects, including language arts and math.</p><p>In 2025, the National Microschooling Center surveyed 800 microschools across the U.S. and found that nearly three-quarters serve neurodivergent students and about half serve children who’ve experienced emotional trauma or have other special needs.</p><p>Melissa Feiger, a microschool founder based in Lincoln Park, runs a program specifically for neurodivergent students. A former public school teacher, Feiger hopes that public schools take note of the personalization and flexibility that microschools can offer.</p><p>“Every kid deserves this type of education,” she said. “They should enjoy learning, they should want to come to school and feel safe. And that’s what microschools are doing right now. We’re showing the traditional system what it could look like.”</p><h3>Ollie Allen, founder of Teach Them How to Learn, a microschool in Hyde Park</h3><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Ollie Allen, of Teach Them How to Learn, looks out of her classroom window at the Hyde Park Neighborhood Club in late October.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Kameron Clepper/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Allen got the inspiration to open her Chicago microschool while she was teaching in Las Vegas. She saw that her students needed more support, so she started offering after-school and summer tutoring. As she worked with third to fifth graders outside the constraints of a typical school day, she realized she could take a different approach to education.</p><p>“Doing the all-day summer program was a full day of learning. And it was so fun,” Allen said. “I saw the light bulbs going off in the kids’ eyes. I saw growth and progress. I saw kids helping other kids to get ideas… That was the picture that I needed to see that this could work.”</p><p>After moving back home to Chicago, she opened Teach Them How to Learn, a microschool that now serves seven students in Hyde Park, including two of her own children. Monthly tuition costs $700. Her students range in age from 8 to 13, and every day looks a little different. On Mondays, students often focus on learning new academic material, while on Wednesdays they engage in hands-on learning, such as culinary activities.</p><p>One of the biggest perks of microschooling, she says, is the ability to be flexible in how she teaches — to go outside for a nature lesson one day and take a field trip to a museum on another.</p><p>“We’re not stuck to one particular curriculum, we’re not stuck in one particular room, we’re not stuck trying to get ready for a test,” Allen said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Her small class size allows Ollie Allen to tailor lessons to her students’ unique interests and needs. If a student is interested in trees, they might learn biology through lessons about nature.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Kameron Clepper/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Every student learns according to an individualized plan. She assesses each student on the skills expected from a child at their grade level using observations and the online learning platform IXL, and then designs a curriculum that may span multiple grade levels.</p><p>Allen incorporates each student’s interests as much as possible. If one child is particularly interested in trees, for instance, she might teach subjects like biology and social studies using nature lessons. Another child with different interests would have lessons that look different. Her goal is for “every kid to feel special at the end of the day and feel like they’re learning at their level,” she said.</p><p>The small class size allows her to come up with these individualized plans. It’s a big difference from how she approached lesson planning in public school, where she often had to break down the same material for many students learning at very different paces.</p><p>“It actually takes me less time to plan for each student than it did when I was in public school,” she said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> She points to one fifth grader who came into her program last year reading at a kindergarten level and doing first-grade math.</p><p>Since then, they’ve made a lot of progress, she said, and are at a fourth grade level in both subjects. They just needed more support, Allen said, and a school setting where they could “practice different subjects multiple times over and over again.”</p><p>Still, there are challenges. For one, the path is not as financially secure as teaching in a school district or private school. More than once, she’s had parents show interest in enrolling their children, only to back out as the school year approached, leaving Allen with a smaller income than she expected.</p><p>Regardless, Allen continues to promote the program and, like Feiger, believes teachers in traditional classrooms could learn from the microschooling model.</p><p>“My goal is to educate future educators on skills that are unique to microschooling, but beneficial for classrooms, too,” she said.</p><h3>LaToya Jackson, a parent who chose a south suburban microschool for her daughter</h3><div class="Enhancement" class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anastasia Busby/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Three years ago, LaToya Jackson was at a loss for how to help her daughter Mahogany.</p><p>After missing preschool due to the pandemic, Mahogany was behind her peers at a Catholic school in Chicago’s south suburbs. Through kindergarten and into first grade, Mahogany struggled to keep up with her class. She was soon having behavioral issues, like trying to leave the classroom without permission, that Jackson hadn’t seen before.</p><p>When she went to the school for help, Jackson was told that Mahogany needed an individualized education program, or an IEP — a learning plan outlining support and accommodations for students with disabilities that’s legally required in public schools. Private schools, on the other hand, are not required to provide them, Jackson learned.</p><p>“They just said that they don’t do IEPs,” Jackson recalled. “They don’t do specialized learning. The classroom is the classroom. Either the kid keeps up or they don’t. And that was pretty much it.”</p><p>Jackson and her husband didn’t know much about the public schools in their area, and they were interested in other options. Through her research, Jackson came across Freestyle Learning, a microschool in south suburban Forest Park that doubles as a support center “for families that want to homeschool, but can’t,” according to their website. Like most microschools, the program charges tuition: $620 a month for full-time students.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure The school’s founder, LaTrece Thomas, helped Mahogany address her anxieties about reading and then worked to improve her reading skills.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anastasia Busby/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>After talking with the school’s founder, LaTrece Thomas, Jackson enrolled Mahogany at Freestyle for the second half of her first grade year. She’s now in her third year at the school, learning alongside eight other students of different ages. During that time, Jackson has seen her now-9-year-old daughter make “amazing improvement,” especially in reading.</p><p>“My daughter couldn’t read, she was struggling [and] we didn't know how to help her,” Jackson said. “My daughter did not need an IEP. She just had a different way of learning, or needed someone to just actually walk her through it and say: ‘This is how it’s done.’”</p><p>Thomas, who has homeschooled children full-time since 2020, remembers that Mahogany was dealing with major anxiety around reading when she first enrolled at Freestyle, triggering the behavioral issues she had at her previous school.</p><p>So Thomas focused first on getting to the root of Mahogany’s anxiety, letting her know it was okay to make mistakes and that her progress would look different from other students’. said. “She no longer has to fake it and act as if she's reading a book. Because now, she knows she’s excited to read.”</p><p>Jackson has noticed that her daughter is more capable of completing assignments independently. She credits the one-on-one help from Thomas paired with opportunities for Mahogany to learn at her own pace.</p><p>But she’s also seen the drawbacks of microschooling. She worries that her daughter isn’t getting a sense of the “real world” — she attends school Monday to Thursday, and now thinks that Fridays are days off, for example.</p><p>Jackson is weighing whether to transfer her daughter to a traditional school in a couple years to see how she does. While it’s been good for Mahogany to learn at her own pace, Jackson knows that when she’s older and in the workforce, that might not be an option.</p><p>“Some jobs are not doing things at your pace,” Jackson said. “They’re saying: ‘These are the timelines, this is when you need to know it by’ or ‘This is when it's done by.’ With Freestyle Learning, if you don't get it, they’re going to stay on it until you get it.”</p>
